title: Git internals and config
idea: Git stores a project as objects named by a hash of their content: blobs are files, trees are folders, and a commit points to a tree.

analogy.text: A warehouse where every box is labelled by a fingerprint of what is inside. Identical contents get the same label, so Git stores them once.
analogy.breaks: Real boxes can be edited; a Git object never changes.

points: A blob holds only a file's bytes. Its name lives in the tree.
A tree lists names, each pointing to a blob or a smaller tree.
A commit adds an author, a message and parent links to a tree.
Settings come from system, global (you), then local (repository); the last wins.

steps.caption: A commit stores the author, the message and a pointer to one tree.
The tree is the project's root folder. It lists each name and points to what it holds.
Two files with equal contents share one blob, because the name lives in the tree.
A subfolder is another tree, which points to its own blobs.
The commit also points to its parent. That link turns commits into a history.

code.title: Read the objects
code.caption: Real Git output. `cat-file` reads any object by name; hashes here come from fixed demo dates.

walk.text: Create a repository with one commit that adds `README.md`.
`-t` prints an object's type. `HEAD` is a commit.
`-p` prints it readably: one tree, one parent, author, committer, message.
The commit's tree lists names: `README.md` is a blob, `src` is another tree.
A blob prints as the file's own text.
Both commits point at the same README blob: equal content is stored once.

code.title: Config levels
code.caption: The name and emails are demo values. Replace them with your own.

walk.text: `--global` writes your own file, usually `~/.gitconfig`: settings for every repository.
Make a repository. It has its own `.git/config`.
Without a flag, `git config` writes this repository's file only.
Reading a key gives the winner: the local value.
`--get-all` lists every value, `--show-origin` adds its file. The last one wins.

pitfalls: Set `user.name` and `user.email` first; existing commits keep the identity they were made with.
Without `--global`, `git config user.name Ada` sets the name for this repository only.
Never put passwords or tokens in `git config`; the files are plain text.

quiz.q: What do the three commands print, in order?
quiz.code:
git cat-file -t HEAD
git cat-file -t 'HEAD^{tree}'
git cat-file -t HEAD:README.md
quiz.why: `HEAD` is a commit, `HEAD^{tree}` is its root tree, and `HEAD:README.md` is one file's blob.

takeaway: Objects are named by their content, so an unchanged file is stored once.

starters: Why does Git name objects by a hash of their content?
